blocks.cap: The last hour of the thin night, the chair asking in a voice that is finally, terribly, Rei's own

blocks.p: The last lantern on the river went out a few metres from the pier. It did not drift away. It simply stopped being lit, and behind it, where the second light had leaned close to watch it, something on the far side let out a breath Rei felt on his face.

His father used to say the truth of any account comes down to a single line. Rei found the line now, standing on the gravel with his chest bowed around the strain of the Axis. The light at the centre could not hold both brothers for much longer. The seam could not stay this open until morning without tearing. And the chair was speaking.

It did not speak in the Healer's voice, or in Gin's. It spoke in Rei's own. That was the thing he had not understood from his notes and understood now in his body. It used the voice he thought in. You could. You fit. Sit down and it stops hurting everyone. A vacant office is not argued into being filled. A living register has to agree to bear it, and the only voice that can agree is the voice of the one who will sit. The Healer could not put him in the chair. The thing watching through Kaito's eyes could not. Gin, with every stolen sentence, could not keep him out.

So the whole month had come to this. Every knot in the ledger, every soft-voiced woman with a bowl of soup, the six-year lean of an empty office on a sleeping ward. All of it had brought him to this rail on this night, and then stepped back, and left him alone with his own voice.

He felt the pulls one after another, the way he had felt the registers in Shin-Ōkubo test his walled places. The warm downward pull of the chair, which felt exactly like being tired enough to lie down in snow. The sick lurch of looking at his brother's hands and thinking, for half a second, he said let it be him, and hating himself for how much lighter the half-second was. The black temptation of simply walking away up the embankment and letting the wall do what walls do when no one holds them. And under all of it something worse and quieter. The Axis was straining in his chest like a rope. He could pull. He could pull until it snapped and the chair came apart with it, and there would be no chair for anyone, only a hole, and no one would ever be made to sit.

"You are counting," the Healer said gently. It was watching his face. "Good. Count. A seat taken is every other seat untaken. A city saved this way is a city not saved that way. A brother kept is a chair left empty. A chair filled is a brother spent. There is no reading of the ledger, however long you stare, in which the columns come out even."
Rei had understood the trap completely. Understanding it did not move him out of it.

He thought about the face at the centre of the light. The tired young man in the old coat, who had answered one question and was now spending himself to keep two strangers off a chair. The seat I became. He thought about the ledger the Healer kept describing, its neat columns. There was no column in it for that man. Every sum the Healer had shown him ended with the man at the centre burning a little more, and the Healer had never once counted him.
And he thought about something the Healer had said a few minutes ago, almost proudly. I only had to let him notice in order.
A thing that needs you to notice in order needs you to be on time.
Rei decided to be late.
"Not tonight," he said.

He said it to the chair first, out loud, in the only voice it would listen to. He felt the question in the seam go unanswered and stay unanswered, like a phone left ringing in an empty flat. Then he said it again, more quietly, to the light. The way a person would tell a man holding a door that he could ease his arms for a moment. Rei stopped leaning on the fulcrum. He stopped asking it for anything.

The Axis felt the demand go out of the night. The bowing in Rei's chest eased by a degree, then another. The light at the centre did not go out. It simply stopped breaking. For a heartbeat, before it sank back toward the wall, Rei thought the face looked at him with something like surprise.
He crossed the gravel to the rail and took his brother's hand.

It was Gin's hand. Cold, too still, and his. Under Rei's thumb the knuckles were faintly raised where the small keys had been inked between them years ago. The Healer let him take it. Rei felt it decide to let him, the way a doctor lets a relative hold a patient's hand on the ward round.
"We're going home," Rei said. "Both of us. You can come too, since you're wearing him. But we're going."
For a long moment the Healer looked at him through Gin's eyes. Then it smiled, the dry half-smile Gin always made and never followed with the joke.

"The ice is only soft tonight," it said. "Tomorrow is the last night. The sending fires. The dead go home and the wall goes thinner than this, and for longer. You have bought one day, Rei. I do not mind. A day is nothing to me." It glanced at the far bank. "It is nothing to that one either. Read your clocks."

Across the river Kaito turned and walked back down the far embankment into the dark, unhurried. Whatever looked out of him had seen enough. The chair would still be open tomorrow, and Kishin could wait one more night as easily as the Healer could.

Rei walked his brother off the embankment as the sky went grey over the yards. They went through the Kita-Ōji sidings, where the old misery in the sheds had stopped leaning and only lay there, and up past the dark hill of Asukayama, and along the shut streets of Ōji. Hand in hand, like boys. Neither of them spoke. Twice Gin's fingers pressed Rei's. Once, then once, then once. The knock from the inside. True, and not the Healer wearing true like a coat.
At the foot of the stairs to the flat, in the first real light, the hand let go.
"I'll be at the rail tonight," the Healer said kindly, in Gin's voice. "So will you."

It turned and walked back the way they had come, in his brother's body and his brother's cardigan. Rei stood at the foot of the stairs and watched until the street bent and took it. Only when it was gone did he look down and see what it had left in his palm when it let go. A square of washi folded small, still warm from his brother's palm, with a single letter pencilled on the outside in Gin's upright hand. R.
